pr_title: Adding per daemon core-dump rate limit
pr_body:
When a daemon gets into a fault condition, it could result in a crash.
The fault condition can stay for a prolonged period of time or it might surface
at a regular interval.  Such scenarios could result in recursive or periodic
crashes of the daemon.  Halon core dump generation module will keep generating
the core dump as long as the space is available.  Once the available core dump
space goes below a threshold, this module will start deleting the older core dump
to provide space for preserving new core dump files.  But this approach would
result in lots of write/erase happening to the storage in case of recursive/
periodic crashes.  This impacts storage endurance and core dump optics.  Hence
the core dump generation should be rate-limited per daemon to avoid continuous
core dump generation in case of a recursive or periodic daemon crash.

Additionally, can we also uses these configurations to rate-limit the coredump per daemon per boot?

### Proposal:
If the RateLimitIntervalSec is set to 0 and RateLimitBurst is set to N, then we can limit to N coredumps per daemon per boot.

In summary, the behavior of these configurations would be as below

| RateLimitIntervalSec | RateLimitBurst | Behavior |
|-----------------------|------------------|-----------|
| 0 | 0 | No rate limit applied |
| T | 0 | No rate limit applied |
| 0 | N | Limited to N core dumps per daemon per boot |
| T | N | Limited to N core dumps per daemon over a period of T seconds |

issue_context.title: Rate limit coredump generation per service
issue_context.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
When a daemon is crashing frequently, we get lots of coredump generated.  Is there a way to rate limit the coredump generation per daemon?
For example, if a daemon is crashing once in every one hour, we will get 24 core dumps generated in a day for that particular daemon.  We want to limit this to 5 core dumps per day per daemon. 

As per our rotation policy, we always delete the oldest core dump whenever the KeepFree/MaxSize limit is hit.  If a problematic daemon is crashing frequently, it might fill up the disk space quickly resulting in cleaning up some older coredump ( which might be belong to some other daemon and might be of interest for our analysis.)  we want to avoid this situation, hence we prefer to rate limit the core dump generation per daemon.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Currently we have the StartLimitIntervalSec, StartLimitBurst to control the restart of the service.  But when the limit is hit, it will stop the service from getting started.  We want the service to be always running even if it crashes frequently, but we want to rate limit the coredump generation alone.
comments: Hmm, that's the same feature you asked for in #17515 already?
Please don't open redundant issues. Will close the other one now.

Hmm, so there are two appraoches here: rate limit *generation* of coredumps, or tweak "vacuuming" of coredumps so that multiple coredumps of the same service are preferably cleaned up.

I think tweaking "vacuuming" is much preferable, since it means that if disk size allow it you actually may retain multiple coredump, but if disk space is scarce we'll priorize properly.

Would tweaking "vacuuming" be sufficient for you?

(or to say this differently: is processing — i.e. compressing and writing to disk — the coredump the issue for you? Or just the disk space taken up? if the former, then ratelimiting of the genreation makes sense. If the latter then tweaking the vacuuming is the better approach I am sure)
We prefer to rate-limit to avoid unnecessary processing and writing to the disk.

> Please don't open redundant issues. Will close the other one now.

Sorry, Initially I thought both are two different features., But I feel that the rate limiting should be sufficient to handle both the scenarios.

This of course then means that if you only want to keep one coredump per service, this would mean you#d retain the oldest, and suppress the newest. With the vacuuming approach we'd do it the other way round: vacuum the oldest, retain the newest coredump for each service.

We want to reduce the amount of writes happening to the storage when some daemon is crashing recursively.  In such cases, the first core dump and the newer core dumps will most probably have the same back trace.  Hence it is ok to ignore the newer core dumps and preserve only the first core dump(practically, we observed that the first core dump provides more information on why we got into that recursive crash situation then the newer core dumps).  Also, once the rate limit interval is over, we will allow the fresh batch of core dumps to be preserved.  For example, if we configure the burst as 3 and interval as 300 seconds, then we will allow to generate up to 3 core dumps once in every 300 seconds for that daemon. So there is possibility of getting newer core dumps also preserved.

In the case of vacuuming approach, every core dump will be written to the storage, so in case of recursive crash it impacts the storage life time.

If time permits, we prefer to have both the solution implemented (rate limiting(high priority) and vacuuming per daemon ) and let the user choose the solution based on the need.
